virt-manager (Virtual Machine Manager) is the most mature graphical management tool in the libvirt ecosystem. It is written in Python and built on GTK; check the dependencies of your installed version. It provides a complete GUI for creating, configuring, monitoring, and managing KVM/QEMU virtual machines, and also supports remote management of hypervisors such as Xen and LXC.

How virt-manager relates to libvirt virt-manager is a client that communicates with the libvirtd daemon through the libvirt API. Whether the hypervisor is local or remote, the underlying call chain is libvirt → libvirtd → QEMU/KVM. Understanding this helps when troubleshooting connection failures.

The dangers of unsafe mode unsafe mode ignores every disk-flush request from the guest. This can greatly accelerate installation or initialization, but an unexpected host power loss in production will cause irrecoverable data corruption. Use it only for temporary tests or disposable VMs in CI pipelines.

Choosing NAT vs. Bridge
NAT is sufficient for development and testing. Choose Bridge mode when other machines on the LAN need to access the VM, for example when hosting a web server.

A snapshot is not a backup A snapshot records a VM's state at a point in time, including disk and memory. It enables quick rollback but cannot replace a backup. The snapshot chain depends on the original disk image: if the underlying qcow2 file is corrupted, all snapshots become unusable. A real backup requires an independent copy of the disk-image file.

4. The hardware configuration panel in detail

Panel settings are configuration choices, not performance guarantees. CPU topology must match the vCPU count. host-model does not guarantee live-migration compatibility across heterogeneous hosts; even with identical CPU models, host-passthrough requires checks of microcode, machine type, QEMU, and devices. Memory current/max settings differ from the hotplug maxMemory/slots settings, and hotplug also requires guest support. raw images can be sparse files; legacy qcow2 AES is not a modern encryption scheme. Multiqueue virtio-net requires compatible guest drivers and settings such as ethtool configuration.

virt-manager's GUI support for virtiofs is limited, so it is usually configured through virsh or by editing the XML directly:

Advantages of virtiofs
viriofs offers significant performance advantages over 9p/virtio-9p and Samba/NFS because it is based on FUSE and passes file operations directly through shared memory, avoiding protocol-conversion overhead. The Linux guest virtiofs driver has been available since 5.4. The host requires matching QEMU, virtiofsd, and libvirt support; checking only the host kernel version is insufficient.

Do not expose unauthenticated libvirt TCP, VNC, or SPICE listeners. Prefer restricting direct display connections to localhost or an SSH tunnel. SPICE OpenGL/virgl usually requires a local Unix socket; do not combine GL configuration fragments with arbitrary remote TCP SPICE examples. TLS must include peer verification and authorization. Monolithic configuration-file examples do not automatically apply to modular daemons or socket activation.

System vs. session connections VMs managed through qemu:///system (system mode) appear in sudo virsh list --all; the identity under which QEMU runs depends on the host configuration. VMs managed through qemu:///session (session mode) run as the current user without sudo, but have limited functionality, such as being unable to use bridged networking. The actual default connection depends on the version, packaging, and existing user settings. Check the connection URI first.
